The Kuleshov effect: show a blank face, then soup, and people say he's hungry. Show a coffin, they say he's sad. Same face. The edit is the acting.
Hitchcock's bomb rule: show the audience the bomb under the table and a boring chat becomes 10 minutes of suspense. Tell them, then make them wait.

A tilted camera, the Dutch angle, tells you the world is wrong before any character says so.
Rule of thirds: put the eyes on the top third line and the frame feels right. You've been seeing it your whole life.
Foley is fake sound made in a studio. That punch you heard was probably someone hitting a cabbage.
Colour tells you how to feel. Teal and orange for action, cold blue for loneliness, warm yellow for memories.
Editing rhythm: fast cuts make you anxious, long takes make you lean in. The editor controls your heartbeat.
Blocking is where actors stand and move. Who's higher, who's closer to the door, who turns away. Power lives in blocking.
Low angle: the character is powerful. High angle: they're small. Directors tell you who's winning before the dialogue does.
Dramatic irony: the audience knows something the character doesn't. That's why you shout at the screen.
A cold open starts in the middle of the action, no intro. It's why the first 30 seconds of a good movie feel like a hook.
Setup and payoff: plant something early, pay it off late. When the payoff hits, the audience feels smart. That's the trick.

text: Here's what nobody tells you about AI video: generating the shot takes minutes. Deciding which shot the story needs, fixing the character so they look the same, adding sound, and cutting it so it feels like a scene takes hours. The audience only sees the 15 seconds.

text: If I could give my younger self one piece of advice about creating: finish things. A finished bad video teaches you more than a perfect video that lives in your drafts forever. Post it, learn, make the next one better.
Ask yourself before every post: would I stop scrolling for this if someone else made it? If the honest answer is no, change the first line or the first frame. You have one second. Make it count.

Hollywood is scared of AI because it threatens what they already have. Small creators in places like Lagos are excited because it gives us what we never had: a way to show the world our stories without waiting for anyone's budget.

Lagos traffic has taught me more about storytelling than film school could: everyone has a goal, something always blocks it, tempers rise, someone does something unexpected, and the ending is never what you planned. Every bus ride is a three-act structure.

People think the hard part of AI filmmaking is the tech. It's not. It's the same thing that's always been hard: having an idea worth watching, and caring enough to make it properly. The tools changed. The hard part didn't.

Thirty days of posting every day: videos, thoughts, questions, the good days and the bad ones. Not to go viral, but to find out what I actually love making when I stop worrying about the numbers. If you're doing the same, let's keep each other going.

Writing a good prompt is like writing a good brief for a film crew: who's in the shot, where they are, what they're doing, where the camera is, and what the light looks like. Vague briefs get vague shots, from humans and machines.

Everyone's chasing realism in AI video. I think style will win. When every tool can make a perfect realistic shot, the only thing that stands out is a look people recognise as yours in one frame. Start building that look now.
